G9A-01-01: Change one variable at a time so you can identify what caused the result.
G9A-02-01: A model represents only the features needed for the investigation.
G9A-03-01: A scientific theory explains observations. It does not become a law as evidence accumulates.
G9A-04-01: Check the difference between milli and micro, and the direction of conversion.
G9A-05-01: For multiplication, use the number of significant figures in the least precise factor.
G9A-06-01: Closely grouped readings can still come from an incorrectly calibrated instrument.
G9A-07-01: Two quantities can increase together without having a linear relationship.
G9A-08-01: You need the time between dots to interpret their spacing.
G9A-09-01: A formula containing force can still give a scalar quantity.
G9A-10-01: The sign of position and the sign of velocity describe different things.
G9A-11-01: Crossing position curves indicate a shared position. Compare their slopes to compare velocities.
G9A-12-01: An average over a journey can differ from the velocity at a particular instant.
G9A-13-01: Positive acceleration can reduce speed when velocity is negative.
G9A-13-02: Touching the time axis indicates a reversal only if velocity also changes sign.
G9A-14-01: Include the initial velocity before adding the change in velocity.
G9A-15-01: Take the square root and use the direction of travel to select the velocity sign.
G9A-16-01: At the top of a free fall trajectory, velocity can be zero while gravitational acceleration continues.
G9A-17-01: Measurement uncertainty can arise from the instrument even with careful technique.
G9A-18-01: Adding displacement magnitudes gives distance on this journey. Use signed displacements for the net change.
G9A-19-01: The height on a position graph gives position. Speed comes from the magnitude of its slope.
G9A-20-01: Negative signed area reduces net displacement but still contributes to total distance.
G9A-20-02: Read the full constant-velocity interval, from 5 s through 15 s.
G9A-20-03: A secant gives an interval average. A tangent gives the instantaneous slope.
G10A-01-01: Measure both angles from the same normal before applying the reflection law.
G10A-02-01: Distinguish the object-to-mirror distance from the separation the question asks for.
G10A-03-01: Trace the rays for a concave mirror. A convex mirror produces different images.
G10A-04-01: Use reciprocal distances in the mirror equation.
G10A-05-01: The sign of magnification gives orientation. Use its absolute value to judge image size.
G10A-06-01: Divide the speed in vacuum by the speed in the medium.
G10A-07-01: At the critical angle the refracted ray follows the surface. Total internal reflection requires a larger angle.
G10A-08-01: Frequency stays fixed across a boundary while speed and wavelength can change.
G10A-09-01: Reflection inside a raindrop can be partial.
G10A-10-01: Trace the rays through a diverging lens before assigning image properties.
G10A-10-02: Image orientation and type can stay the same even as image height changes.
G10A-11-01: Spherical aberration depends on where a ray passes through the lens.
G10A-12-01: Match the corrective lens to the location of the image relative to the retina.
G10A-13-01: For a bright interference fringe, check the required whole-wavelength path difference.
G10A-14-01: Include both reflected waves and the extra distance travelled within the film.
G10A-15-01: A reflection grating needs regularly spaced grooves.
G10A-16-01: Use the positions of spectral lines to identify the element.
G10A-17-01: Here a negative image distance places a virtual image behind the mirror.
G10A-18-01: In this example, a critical angle applies to travel from glass into air.
G10A-18-02: Use the sine of the angle in Snell’s law.
G10A-19-01: Convert millimetres and nanometres to a common unit.
G10A-20-01: Convert line density to line spacing by taking the reciprocal.
G11A-01-01: Check the direction of the conversion by converting half a revolution.
G11A-02-01: All points share angular speed. Linear speed varies with distance from the axis.
G11A-03-01: The product of angular acceleration and radius gives only the tangential component.
G11A-04-01: Distinguish cycles per second, seconds per cycle and radians per second.
G11A-05-01: Points at different radii can have equal angular speed and different linear speeds.
G11A-06-01: Assign torque signs using the direction each force tends to turn the object.
G11A-06-02: A force parallel to the arm has zero moment about its pivot.
G11A-07-01: Calculate mass times radius squared for each particle before adding.
G11A-08-01: Assess the centre of mass and support base when judging stability.
G11A-09-01: A couple can produce zero net force and a nonzero torque.
G11A-10-01: Apparent deflection in a rotating frame does not require an additional contact force.
G11A-11-01: The action and reaction act on different bodies. Draw one free-body diagram at a time.
G11A-12-01: Use the full duration of the force pulse when calculating impulse.
G11A-13-01: An object can gain momentum by ejecting mass in empty space.
G11A-14-01: A cushion changes the stopping time while the required momentum change remains.
G11A-15-01: Check angular momentum conservation separately from kinetic energy conservation.
G11A-16-01: A constant angular momentum allows moment of inertia and angular speed to change together.
G11A-17-01: Rotational equilibrium still requires a separate check for translational equilibrium.
G11A-18-01: Choose the moment of inertia for the given shape and rotation axis.
G11A-18-02: Mass distribution matters even for objects with identical mass and radius.
G11A-19-01: Use signed velocities in the change of momentum.
G11A-20-01: Objects that stick together lose some kinetic energy in a collision with relative motion.
G12A-01-01: When gravitational potential energy increases, gravity does negative work.
G12A-02-01: A deformed spring stores elastic potential energy.
G12A-03-01: Energy can change form. Sticking together is one special case of an inelastic collision.
G12A-04-01: A wavelength-spectrum peak and a frequency-spectrum peak cannot be converted directly by dividing c by the peak wavelength.
G12A-05-01: Use the energy difference between states for a transition.
G12A-06-01: In the single-photon model here, one photon must supply the energy to release an electron.
G12A-07-01: At fixed frequency, increasing intensity increases the photon rate while each photon keeps the same energy.
G12A-08-01: Subtract the work function from photon energy to find maximum electron kinetic energy.
G12A-09-01: A photon carries momentum even though its rest mass is zero.
G12A-10-01: Matter wavelength decreases as momentum increases.
G12A-11-01: The uncertainty relation constrains the simultaneous spreads of position and momentum.
G12A-12-01: A nuclear model alone cannot account for atomic stability or discrete spectral lines.
G12A-13-01: A line spectrum contains distinct wavelengths with gaps between them.
G12A-14-01: A bound state can have negative energy while the emitted photon has positive energy.
G12A-15-01: Identify the spectral series from the final level.
G12A-16-01: Distinguish spontaneous emission with random phase from stimulated emission.
G12A-17-01: Omitting rotational kinetic energy overestimates the final translational speed.
G12A-18-01: Total momentum can be conserved while kinetic energy changes.
G12A-19-01: Convert electronvolts to joules before comparing the numerical slope with Planck’s constant in J·s.
G12A-19-02: Read the vertical axis carefully. Current and maximum kinetic energy give different graphs.
G12A-20-01: Subtract the level energies and keep full precision until the final result.
